fields.foundation: The Hittites established themselves on the Anatolian plateau during the early second millennium BCE, absorbing the indigenous Hattian population, whose religious traditions and royal titles they largely inherited. The Old Kingdom emerged around 1650 BCE under Hattusili I, who made Hattusa his capital, a naturally defensible site among the rocky highlands of north-central Anatolia, and campaigned southward into Syria. His successor Mursili I raided Babylon around 1595 BCE and ended the First Babylonian Dynasty. It was the dynasty's boldest early venture and reached far beyond its base, but it brought no permanent territorial gain. A period of palace murders and coups followed, recounted in the Edict of Telipinu around 1525 BCE, which showed how fragile early Hittite kingship was. The New Hittite Kingdom reached its full strength under Suppiluliuma I (c. 1344–1322 BCE), who made the Hittites a great power competing directly with Egypt and Mitanni for control of the Levantine corridor. He dismantled the Mitanni kingdom and installed Hittite-aligned rulers across Syria, including his own sons at Carchemish and Aleppo, and so established the imperial framework of the empire at its height.
fields.socioeconomy: The Hittite economy rested on the agriculture of the Anatolian plateau, supplemented by herding and by the working of substantial metal deposits, particularly copper and silver. The Hittites held a strategically important position astride the routes connecting Mesopotamia to the Aegean, and merchants working under Hittite protection took part in the long-distance tin and copper trade that supplied the ancient world's bronze industry. Land was formally held by the palace and the temples and distributed to warriors, officials and cultivators in return for military service or labour obligations, an arrangement documented in detailed land-grant texts. The state stored and redistributed grain through royal magazines, as a buffer against the harvest failures to which the plateau was prone. Tribute from vassal states in Syria and western Anatolia added significantly to agricultural revenues, so the empire's finances depended directly on its outlying vassal network. The loss of Syrian vassals to Egyptian or Assyrian competition therefore meant immediate fiscal damage as well as the loss of territory.
fields.military: The Hittite army was built around the chariot as its main offensive arm. It used heavier three-man vehicles carrying a driver, a shield-bearer and a spearman, in contrast to the lighter two-man Egyptian designs, and so favoured shock and close combat over mobile archery. The Battle of Kadesh in 1274 BCE, fought against Ramesses II on the Orontes River under Muwatalli II, is often described as the largest chariot engagement of antiquity, with perhaps five thousand chariots involved on both sides. Neither side won a decisive victory, though both claimed triumph, and Kadesh itself remained in Hittite hands. Hittite infantry combined levies and professional palace troops with vassal contingents, which gave numbers but variable reliability. In his Syrian campaigns Suppiluliuma I combined direct military action with diplomatic subversion, detaching enemy vassals before engaging their principals. The Hittites conducted systematic siege warfare, with battering rams and siege works described in the Old Hittite account of the siege of Urshu, though their preferred method remained political isolation rather than costly direct assault.
fields.governance: The Hittite political system centred on the Great King at Hattusa, whose authority was at once military, judicial and religious. Unlike the Egyptian pharaoh, the Hittite king was not a living god but the earthly steward of the storm god Tarhun, and became divine only after death. The relationship between royal and priestly authority was therefore more negotiated. The empire managed its periphery through a tiered vassal system, with subordinate rulers bound by formal treaties specifying military obligations, tribute and diplomatic restrictions. These vassal treaties, which survive in substantial numbers from the Hattusa archives, are one of the ancient world's most developed bodies of international law. The Hittite legal code, preserved on two tablets, was less brutal than contemporary Mesopotamian equivalents and favoured compensation and restitution over mutilation and death. Members of the royal family held the main provincial positions, concentrating power within the dynasty but creating recurring succession tensions that periodically destabilised the central government.
fields.impact: The Treaty of Kadesh, concluded between Hattusili III and Ramesses II around 1259 BCE, is the earliest peace treaty to survive in the versions of both parties: in Akkadian cuneiform at Hattusa and in Egyptian hieroglyphs at Karnak and the Ramesseum. A replica hangs today at the United Nations headquarters in New York. The diplomatic correspondence found at Amarna and Hattusa documents great-power relations among the Hittites, Egypt, Babylon, Assyria and Mitanni, conducted in Akkadian as the Bronze Age international language. Anatolian ironworking contributed to the gradual diffusion of iron technology across the Near East. Religious and literary traditions absorbed from the Hattians and Hurrians were transmitted westward, and the Hurro-Hittite Kumarbi cycle, with its succession of warring sky gods, closely parallels Hesiod's Theogony, one of the earliest documented channels of cultural transmission between the Near East and Europe.
fields.decline: The Hittite Empire collapsed in the early twelfth century BCE as part of the broader Bronze Age Collapse, which destroyed or crippled most of the major states of the eastern Mediterranean within a generation. The Sea Peoples, migrating confederacies whose raids disrupted the coastal trade networks on which the Late Bronze Age international system depended, are traditionally cast as the immediate agents, though their exact role remains debated. Hattusa was abandoned and burned around 1180 BCE under the last known king, Suppiluliuma II, and never again served as a royal capital. Other factors were succession conflicts around the reign of Tudhaliya IV, prolonged drought and famine documented in correspondence requesting emergency grain shipments from Egypt, and the fragmentation of the vassal network that had sustained imperial revenues. Assyrian expansion westward added pressure on the eastern frontier. Neo-Hittite city-states in northern Syria and south-eastern Anatolia, including Carchemish and Malatya, preserved elements of Hittite political and artistic tradition for centuries before they were absorbed into the Assyrian Empire. They were an epilogue to the civilisation rather than its continuation.
fields.summary: The Hittite Empire showed that great-power competition could be managed through formal diplomacy as effectively as through military force. The Treaty of Kadesh is a model of negotiated international order, and its conceptual descendants remain foundational to international law today.
fields.teaser: The Hittites were ancient Anatolia's dominant power and early workers of iron. After their battle with Egypt at Kadesh in 1274 BCE, the rivals concluded around 1259 BCE the earliest peace treaty surviving in both sides' versions.
fields.t0: A Bronze Age power ruled from Hattusa in central Anatolia that rivalled Egypt for control of Syria and the Levant.
fields.t1: Its vassal treaties and its peace with Ramesses II are among the earliest milestones of international law and diplomacy.
fields.t2: It vanished in the Bronze Age Collapse when Hattusa was abandoned and burned c. 1180 BCE; Neo-Hittite city-states carried on its legacy.
fields.dyk: A replica of the Hittite-Egyptian peace treaty, the earliest to survive in both parties' versions, hangs at the United Nations headquarters in New York.
